bibliography.abstract: This article explores how women’s everyday care for street dogs in Eskişehir generates more-than-human solidarities through which urban space is reclaimed and produced. In this context, solidarity is conceptualized as an embodied and situated process of becoming-with, shaped by questions of legitimacy, vulnerability, and spatial belonging. Drawing on qualitative interviews, the study shows that under patriarchal and human-centred socio-spatial orders, relations of care between women and street dogs can take on solidaristic forms that intervene in the social production of space. Here, more-than-human solidarity emerges as a reciprocal process in which women struggle to render street dogs legitimate co-habitants of the city, while street dogs transform women’s experiences of urban space, enabling them to reclaim spaces and temporalities they would otherwise avoid. Contributing to feminist geography and more-than-human urbanism, the article relies on a relational understanding of the social production of urban space, foregrounding everyday multispecies solidarities through which fragile yet meaningful claims to the city are enacted.
bibliography.title: Reclaiming the city: more-than-human solidarities between women and street dogs in Eskişehir

en.caveats: The findings are based on qualitative interviews in a single city, focusing on specific gendered and cultural dynamics that may not directly translate to other urban contexts.
en.what: Through qualitative interviews in Eskiřehir, Turkey, this study examines how everyday care practices between women and street dogs shape the social production of urban space. It documents a reciprocal relationship where women advocate for the legitimacy of street dogs as urban co-habitants, while the presence of the dogs alters women's spatial experiences, allowing them to access and reclaim urban areas and times of day they would otherwise avoid due to safety concerns.
en.why: The study demonstrates that urban solidarity and space-making are not exclusively human activities, showing how multispecies relationships can actively disrupt and reshape patriarchal and anthropocentric urban structures.
